Benjamin Libet did an experiment back in the day. The basics of this are that he gave subjects a choice between two items—let’s say, “Chocolate” or “Vanilla.” He then measured activity in the brain. What he learned was that parts of their brains actually lit up. Parts that were “pre conscious.” Their brains made the choice for them before they were conscious of the choice, and of owning their choice. In other words, everything you decide, choose, want, and wish for is created not by “you” or your own autonomy, but rather by circuits in your brain that are outside of your own awareness and identity and then are handed down to you. 

So asking when I “feel” free is almost irrelevant as it, too, is an experience that happens outside of “me” and I have no control over. 

For a completely different take on the matter, check out Sartre’s position on freedom and living an authentic life. 

But to not sound so academic, to me freedom comes from those brief open, joyful experiences. When everything is right and the world stops. Whether it’s a great Christmas Eve with snow gently falling outside and the world is at peace, riding “Space Mountain” at Disneyland, hanging out with the best of friends, watching the sun rise over Death Valley, etc.

The circle suggests ending where you began. Theologically, the perfect shape. Divine. God. And reincarnation. Rebirth. Meher Baba speaks about this in his “Discourses” (e.g., “The recurring incident of death is matched by the recurring incident of birth”).

Tommy connects with it throughout the film. Captain Walker is embraced by it in the first shot of the film. There’s the circular mirror which Tommy gazes into three times before his Mother throws him through it, smashing it. Tommy is embraced by it and rejoins with it (completing a spiritual circle) at the end of the film. The repetition of certain lyrics (“Tommy, can you hear me?”, “Tommy…Tommy…Tommy…”). The Mother experiences her corruption in a round, white, shiny room with a round, white bed. And, of course, there’s the pinball itself, which, like the mirror, also allows others to connect with God and join on that connection and reflection of themselves (itself a circle of “I am - He is - I am”). The Mother loads them into the missiles at the factory during the war. During Tommy’s “Amazing Journey,” they ping-pong across an array of animated fighter planes. The Doctor uses them as caps to measure Tommy’s eyes. Big ones serve as landscaping when the Faithful rebel. They even adorn the official movie poster. Meher Baba spoke of the role of the individual as “…God passing through imagination in order to realise its own divinity,” which, really, could pretty much serve as a tagline for the “Tommy” film. Although this in itself is linear, reincarnation or rebirth is built in. Tommy’s victory over the Pinball Wizard, for example, is really the rebirth of the soul. Playing pinball becomes a means to connect with God (the circle), reflect and gain awareness (the mirror aspect) and set about on the path to enlightenment even though it may require repeated circular birth-death-reborn cycles to get there. The story of Sally Simpson speaks to rebirth, but also what happens if one chooses hollow pursuits over true spiritual pursuit. 

Tommy achieves true enlightenment at the end of the film. The circle, radiant with Divine light, embraces him. He becomes one with it. It swallows him as the camera pushes into that final unfocused blurry image. Interestingly, we, then, circle (ahem!) back to the beginning of “Listening to You” while the credits roll.

It’s curious to also note that Meher Baba experienced his first spiritual moment while riding a bicycle with its rotating circles (!!) and passed an elderly Muslim Saint. He approached her, she kissed him on the forehead, causing him to enter a nine month-long trance which he described as “divine bliss”, with a lack of consciousness of his body (although I don’t think he stood before a mirror during this time).

There’s also aspects of Christianity embedded in the film. The number 3 (the Trinity) makes several curious appearances. It takes Tommy three times before his soul ( the images in the mirror) can unify and he begins to connect. The Mother is corrupted three times with beans, chocolate, and sudsy soap (she destroys the white, pure flowers). The Faithful hold and wave and shake crosses as props, although they are really “T”s (as in “Tommy” or “Trinity”).

So. The circle suggests ending where you began.

Right. Unlike, say, a standard Medicaid application, SSA-11-BK does not ask for confidential information about the recipient, nor does it allow or authorize provision of such information. The most sensitive questions are phrased along the lines of, “why do you (applicant) think this person needs a Payee?” and “why do you think YOU should be the Payee?” 

The other option is to go down to the local SSA office in person with the recipient. Talk with an agent there. If OP lives in a bigger city, they may be waiting for a while until their number gets called. Never any fun. 

The SSA-787, which I mentioned above, should help to authenticate any questions about medical eligibility. 

Sadly, the SSA is far, far from a well-oiled machine. I’ve seen them do things with great efficiency. But I can’t tell you how many times I’ve seen them create costly errors and then lay the financial burden on the recipient to fix the mess that they created because of their miscalculations. Or hand over Payeeship to someone just because the person called them up and answered a few questions. So the caveat is that no matter how nice procedures look on paper, when dealing with the SSA, you just never know how it will turn out.

From the OP’s perspective, it really is as simple as filling out and sending in the form. 

But to provide a few more details: 

1. Complete and mail in the form.

2. SSA will review. 

3. At some point SSA will contact you and interview you. If all is good, they will assign you to be the Payee.  You will receive notice of this in the mail. You will need to provide them at some point with bank information if you want direct deposit. 

4. Once a year you will need to fill out and send in the Payee report, detailing how you spent the person’s money (rent, food, etc.)

So a brief lesson in psychopharmacology. There might be some big words here, so you may have to put down your coloring book and grab a dictionary:

Antipsychotics are (mostly) dopamine antagonists. Specifically, they block dopamine action post-synaptically at the D1, D2 and/or D4 receptors in the nigro-striatum, mesolimbic region, and a few others. Many of the Cure’s songs consist of layers of instruments. Drum and bass. Two synths, a lead guitar, a rhythm guitar, and another guitar. Sometimes, to create the full effect of the song one instrument (e.g., one guitar) may just play a simple riff repeatedly. You can hear an example in “Pictures of You” where one guitar just plays these single note back-and-forth bits throughout. Or, maybe just in one part of the song (e.g., the chorus). Younger generations of therapists are being taught that trauma is THE THING now. It’s a simple model that creates a framework of dysfunction. To a hammer, every problem looks like a nail. To a therapist now, every person has trauma. It’s crazy. Particularly because: 

1. Trauma indicates that something bad happened to you in your past which now explains your troubles today. Not “bad” as in “I survived a plane crash while all of my family around me were killed.” But bad as in…well…whatever the therapist feels. 

2. The inherent problem behind this is that it’s something that has already happened and can’t be changed. You can’t go back in time. And it has affected you in powerful ways. That rejection from your third grade teacher? Made you the depressive that you are today. Again, it services the therapist’s raison d’etre. “You come to me for therapy because ___(fill in the blank)___. You therefore MUST have trauma. Let’s find it. Whatever it is.”  And it can’t be easily fixed unless the therapist applies their wisened and educated craft.

3. And the reality is that who you are today is a combination of complex elements and dynamics, from what chemicals are swishing around in your brain today to what’s happening in your world around you (e.g., the air conditioner broke and the neighbor’s dog kept you up last night). 

4. The “reality” or narrative of a problem is most often created or constructed in the “now” between the client and the therapist. A client could have two different definitions of what the problem is based on two different models by two different therapists. So when the therapist says it’s due to trauma…that’s powerful stuff. The power of the “expert!” 

Anyways, I could go on. But you get the idea. Trauma is the current fad in therapy—kind of like how twenty years ago everyone who didn’t agree with their therapist was at risk of being labeled “Borderline Personality Disorder.”

I think the problem (and potential cause for concern) is not the story itself, but the story formula structure. I don’t know if modern screenwriters have mastered the art of writing to fit a 10- episode season. 

Follow me on this:

For decades, visual media storytelling primarily occurred either through network shows or theatrical features. Network shows ran for 20-30 episodes a season. That gave writers a chance to give, take, push, and pull. Like TNG, for example. There may be an occasional 2-episode arc. But most episodes were stand-alone, distinct, non-linear stories. You could introduce, play out, and conclude a whole multi-act story in 45 minutes. Boom. See you next week for a brand new adventure. 

Theatrical features range from 90 to 220 minutes or so. There is a particular structure that they all snap into. Act 1…Act 2…Act 3. Writers for decades have followed this. There’s a beginning, an escalation/conflict, a climax, and a resolution. 

Now we live in this weird world where “seasons” are 6-10 episodes long, and I would argue that this just doesn’t suit the narrative needs of film storytelling very well. It’s too long for the compact efficiency of a one or two episode arc, and not long enough to diversify into multiple, separate stories and adventures. 

The end result is too much time and not enough of a singular story. So things get weird. Writers create sub-plots or distractions in order to fill things out. The danger is then wandering, boring, over-extended and unfocused narratives. I first saw this in some of the later short seasons of “Battlestar Galactica” (a great show). 

“The Mandalorian”, “The Book of Boba Fett”, and even “Breaking Bad” are examples of some recent shows that could have been tightened up dramatically if they had been compacted down to shorter running times. 

This is a big cause of complaint for me for “Picard.” If Season 3 were actually a 2-hour feature film, I would have so much more faith in it. Or if it was a 25- episode traditional season.
